title: Advanced Component Patterns: Compound, Slot, & Controlled Abstraction
description: Master enterprise-grade React component patterns: Compound Components with Context, Slot Pattern for flexible composition, Controlled/Uncontrolled abstraction, and Renderless headless UI architecture.

data.text: Component API Design for Reusable Enterprise UI

Building reusable React components for enterprise design systems requires deliberate API design. The naive approach—a monolithic component with 20+ optional boolean props—creates what the React community calls 'prop soup'. Professional component libraries employ structural patterns that separate behavior from presentation, enable flexible composition, and preserve strict TypeScript type safety at every layer.

data.caption: Component Design Pattern Spectrum: From Rigid to Fully Flexible
data.code:
flowchart LR
    A["Monolith Component (Prop Soup)"] -->|More Control| B["Controlled Component (Explicit state prop + onChange)"]
    B -->|More Composition| C["Compound Component (Implicit shared Context)"]
    C -->|More Flexibility| D["Slot Pattern (Children composition + named slots)"]
    D -->|Full Decoupling| E["Headless / Renderless Component (Logic only, no styles)"]

data.text: Compound components allow a parent to implicitly share state with related children, keeping the consuming JSX readable while hiding complexity. The chat message component in an AI assistant is a perfect candidate: the root `ChatMessage` component manages expansion/citation state, and child components (`ChatMessage.Content`, `ChatMessage.Citations`, `ChatMessage.Actions`) consume it via Context without prop drilling.

data.title: Compound ChatMessage Component with TypeScript
data.content: The root component and its children share state via a typed Context. Consumer JSX is clear and readable.

data.text: A well-designed component should work both as 'uncontrolled' (managing its own internal state for simple use cases) and 'controlled' (deferring to an external state owner for integration with forms, Zustand, or React Query). This mirrors the native HTML input's behavior.

data.title: Dual-Mode Controlled/Uncontrolled Component
data.content: The ConversationFilter component works stand-alone with its own state, or can be controlled externally.

data.text: Headless components (popularized by Radix UI, Headless UI, and TanStack) separate behavior from rendering entirely. The component provides interaction logic, keyboard navigation, ARIA attributes, and accessibility wiring—while exposing zero HTML or CSS. Consumers compose any markup they want around the behavior.

data.caption: Component Pattern Comparison: Trade-offs in Flexibility and Complexity
rows: Simple one-off components with stable requirements
Related UI groups like Accordion, Tab panels, Menus
Form fields, filters, selectors needing integration
Layout shells, Card containers, Dialog frames
Design system libraries with custom branded styling

data.title: Component API Design Quality Checklist
items: Components with >5 boolean props are candidates for compound or slot refactoring
All Compound Component sub-components throw a descriptive error if used outside their Context
Controlled components accept value + onChange; uncontrolled fallback uses defaultValue + useState
Every interactive element has explicit aria-label, aria-expanded, or role attributes
Design system components are tested with Testing Library, asserting semantic HTML not CSS class names
TypeScript discriminated unions prevent prop combinations that create impossible component states

data.title: Summary & Next Steps
points: Compound Components with Context eliminate prop drilling in related UI structures.
Dual-mode Controlled/Uncontrolled APIs make components reusable across simple and complex scenarios.
Headless/Renderless components provide maximum flexibility for design system consumers.
Next, we master TypeScript generics for building type-safe, composable utilities.
data.takeaway: Great component design is API design: choose the minimal pattern that satisfies the use case without premature complexity, and preserve strict TypeScript safety at every layer.
